Figure 13-55: Example Plot of Unit Load Transfer Curves
Figure 13-56: Data from an Instrumented Field Load Test
sections.applicability: Converting strain gauge data to load transfer

sections.title: Other Instrumentation
sections.body: [p. 13-62] Accelerometers on or in the shaft for rapid or dynamic tests (high frequency for impact, lower for rapid) give inertial resistance and, by integration, velocity (used in signal matching) and displacement, useful only for short-duration changes referenced to a known displacement; they cannot measure static displacement. Earth pressure cells, rarely used (usually research) at the base, have limited usefulness because the base pressure distribution is unknown and variable. (PDF outline number: 13.2.3.3.)
key_points: Accelerometers: inertia, velocity, short-term displacement only
Base pressure cells of limited use
sections.applicability: Accelerometers and pressure cells in load tests

sections.title: Interpretation of Axial Test Results for Design
sections.body: [pp. 13-62 to 13-63] Test results must be evaluated to estimate design parameters, considering variations in properties and production shaft behavior across the site and differences between design load cases and tested conditions. Compare unit side and base resistance with the geomaterial properties at the test location using a design method (Chapter 10 or local practice), consider adjusting empirical parameters, and use the 'calibrated' correlation for production shafts in similar conditions, with judgment on geology and variability. Where scour, grade changes or groundwater fluctuation change stratigraphy and effective stress, judgment is needed since some empirical correlations do not account for (post-construction) stress changes. Even in cohesionless soil, scour does not reduce horizontal stress proportionally: Delta sigma_h = K (Delta sigma_v) (Eq. 13-9), K the earth pressure coefficient for unloading, leaving a higher OCR and sigma_h greater in proportion to sigma_v than before scour. Intact rock is unlikely to be much affected by short term confinement changes (cementation or bond), but decomposed rock or frictional joints may be sensitive to long term effective stress reduction, to be evaluated from geology and rock mass behavior.
key_points: Calibrate the design method to the test location, then apply to similar locations
Account for scour, grade or groundwater changes with judgment
Delta sigma_h = K Delta sigma_v (Eq. 13-9): unloading leaves higher OCR
Intact rock little affected; decomposed rock or joints may be sensitive
equations: Eq. 13-9: Delta sigma_h = K (Delta sigma_v) - change in horizontal stress at the shaft/soil interface for a change in vertical stress on unloading (scour); K earth pressure coefficient for unloading
sections.applicability: Using axial load test results in design

sections.title: Load Tests to Measure Lateral Resistance
sections.body: [p. 13-63] Drilled shafts are often chosen for their flexural strength and lateral resistance; where lateral loading dominates design, lateral load tests may validate or improve the design models. Overview of planning, methods, instrumentation and interpretation (13.3.1 to 13.3.4).
key_points: Lateral load tests validate or improve lateral design models where lateral loading dominates
sections.applicability: Lateral load test planning and p-y curve calibration

sections.title: General Considerations in Planning Lateral Load Tests
sections.body: [p. 13-63] As with axial testing, establish objectives and define the program considering the production shafts the test models. The page numbers the subheadings 13.3.1.3 to 13.3.1.9; the PDF outline numbers them 13.3.1.1 to 13.3.1.7.
key_points: Objectives and details defined against the production shafts
sections.applicability: Planning lateral load tests on drilled shafts

sections.title: Overall Objectives
sections.body: [pp. 13-63 to 13-64] Lateral test objectives usually concern the design soil models most critical to performance, identified in design (Block 10, Chapter 8) by sensitivity studies; most lateral resistance comes from shallow strata, but if the governing case includes scour the test must evaluate deeper strata. Measuring response along the shaft may be very important to find the distribution of soil resistance. Model the test shaft response so the test evaluates the soil resistance relevant to production; top load, moment and rotational restraint are generally not important, as the objective is the soil model and parameters, and the test shaft may be stronger than production shafts to mobilize more resistance.
key_points: Objective: verify the lateral soil model and parameters, usually shallow strata (deeper with scour)
Measure response along the shaft; head conditions need not match production
Test shaft may be structurally stronger than production shafts
sections.applicability: Defining lateral load test objectives

sections.title: Location and Number of Test Shafts
sections.body: [p. 13-64] Location and number considerations are similar to axial tests; large projects may test several representative 'sites', and an axial test shaft can be laterally tested after its axial test, generally economically.
key_points: Like axial tests; reuse axial test shafts for lateral tests economically
sections.applicability: Locating lateral load test shafts

sections.title: GeoMaterial Properties at Test Location
sections.body: [p. 13-64] Determine the properties of the geomaterials most influencing lateral response, identified by a pre-test model, so their strength and stiffness can be correlated with measured resistance; these layers may differ from those governing axial resistance.
key_points: Pre-test model identifies the strata governing lateral response; investigate them
sections.applicability: Characterizing ground for lateral load tests

sections.title: Scour or Changes in Overburden Stress Conditions
sections.body: [pp. 13-64 to 13-65] Scour and stratigraphy or stress changes affect lateral resistance even more than axial. With deep scour, a test in an unscoured profile may only test scourable strata and be of little use; a test in a large excavated cofferdam (Figure 13-57, right) can be representative, but an isolation casing (left) is not, since overburden confines the soil and prevents a passive wedge, and the casing and intervening soil resistance are hard to isolate. Lateral tests may not be practical, economical or useful where deep scour is anticipated unless similar soils are found near the surface; otherwise conservative parameters may be appropriate.
key_points: Scour affects lateral resistance more than axial
Isolation casing does not represent scour; a large cofferdam may
Where impractical, use conservative design parameters
figures: Figure 13-57: Schematic Diagram of Lateral Test where Scourable Overburden is Present
sections.applicability: Scour effects on lateral load test planning

sections.title: Construction of Test Shaft
sections.body: [p. 13-65] Oversized temporary casing and the resulting shaft-soil contact in shallow strata matter little axially but greatly laterally: a gap around a casing left in an oversized hole should be grouted as in production, and casing left in place adds flexural stiffness that must be modeled.
key_points: Shallow contact governs lateral response: grout gaps as in production
Model any casing left in place in the stiffness
sections.applicability: Constructing lateral load test shafts

sections.title: Use of Prototype Shafts
sections.body: [p. 13-65] Smaller-diameter prototypes are generally not recommended for lateral tests: they are influenced by shallower soils, and flexural stiffness varies with the 4th power of diameter, so they cannot transfer stress to the depths a larger production shaft influences.
key_points: Prototype (smaller) shafts not recommended for lateral tests; stiffness ~ D^4
sections.applicability: Prototype shafts in lateral load tests

sections.title: Group Considerations
sections.body: [p. 13-65] Group effects on lateral response (Chapter 11) typically modify p-y curves for overlapping passive zones; since tests are usually on isolated shafts, the derived model must be modified for groups, whose shafts transfer more load to deeper strata.
key_points: Modify the single-shaft lateral model for group effects (Chapter 11)
sections.applicability: Group effects in interpreting lateral load tests

sections.title: Test Methods and Procedures
sections.body: [p. 13-66] Most lateral tests are conventional static tests jacking the shaft with a hydraulic cylinder, but rapid and bi-directional methods have advantages in some circumstances. The page numbers the subheadings 13.3.2.3 to 13.3.2.5; the PDF outline numbers them 13.3.2.1 to 13.3.2.3.
key_points: Conventional static, bi-directional and rapid lateral tests
sections.applicability: Lateral load test methods

sections.title: Conventional Static Lateral Load Test
sections.body: [pp. 13-66 to 13-68] The shaft is pushed away from, or pulled toward, one or more reaction shafts or piles (ASTM D 3966-07), load measured by a load cell beside the jack; jacking two shafts apart measures both. Figure 13-58: a 30-inch shaft jacked from a beam spanning two reaction shafts, pushed about 3 inches by about 50 tons in stiff clay. Rotation at the shaft tops changes alignment, so a bearing or clevis bracket must avoid eccentricity and the risk of plates popping out; pulled shafts must be far enough apart that passive zones do not overlap. Figure 13-59: clevis bracket and load cell (Kansas DOT shaft with a rectangular extension and steel plate). Figure 13-60: two-way cyclic loading with a programmed double-acting ram following a deflection-time curve, pinned connections, one shaft with a permanent steel liner, relevant for seismic or extreme events (Brown et al., 2002); casing eases welded connections and adds stiffness.
key_points: Push or pull against reaction shafts per ASTM D3966-07; load cell at the jack
Clevis bracket or bearing accommodates head rotation safely
Keep pulled shafts far enough apart to avoid overlapping passive zones
Cyclic two-way tests for seismic or extreme event cases
figures: Figure 13-58: Conventional Static Lateral Load Test Setup
Figure 13-59: Clevis Bracket and Load Cell Mount for Lateral Loading
Figure 13-60: Cyclic Lateral Load Test Setup
sections.applicability: Conventional static lateral load tests

sections.title: Bi-Directional Testing
sections.body: [pp. 13-68 to 13-69] A load cell inserted vertically in a rock socket and cast in concrete jacks the two socket halves apart (O'Neill et al., 1997); load per unit length = cell load / test socket length (about the length of the steel plates). Figure 13-61: a 6-ft socket in sandstone about 100 ft deep, and paired cells in an 8-ft, 15-ft long socket in chalk about 60 ft deep, jacked independently for equal displacement; sacrificial LVDTs measure plate opening. It is not a flexural test but an in-situ test of a formation's lateral resistance at shaft scale, useful for deep strata loaded by groups or exposed by scour, with interpretation accounting for overburden removal.
key_points: Vertical cell splits a rock socket: in-situ lateral resistance of a deep formation
Load per unit length = cell load / socket length
Account for overburden removal or scour in interpretation
figures: Figure 13-61: Bi-directional Lateral Testing Apparatus
sections.applicability: Bi-directional lateral tests in rock sockets

sections.title: Rapid Load Test
sections.body: [p. 13-69] A rapid load device on skids beside the shaft applies a ground-level shear pulse (O'Neill et al. 1997; Rollins et al. 1997), avoiding a reaction system, with lateral loads in excess of 1,000 tons for full size large shafts (Figure 13-62); it may suit rapid or impact design loads (seismic, vessel, ice). Brown (2007) describes an analysis accounting for inertia and rate effects.
key_points: Rapid lateral pulse over 1,000 tons without a reaction system
Suited to rapid or impact design loads; analysis per Brown (2007)
figures: Figure 13-62: Rapid Lateral Load Test
sections.applicability: Rapid lateral load tests

sections.title: Instrumentation
sections.body: [p. 13-70] Lateral test instrumentation is largely as for axial tests; aspects specific to lateral testing follow. The page numbers the subheadings 13.3.3.3 to 13.3.3.5; the PDF outline numbers them 13.3.3.1 to 13.3.3.3.
key_points: Mostly as for axial tests
sections.applicability: Instrumentation for lateral load tests

sections.title: Measurement of Load
sections.body: [p. 13-70] Jacks and load cells as in axial tests, but the jack must work horizontally without leaks and the connection must accommodate significant rotation (the text cites Section 13.3.2.1, as printed); loads are often smaller but displacements much larger. Load cells are preferred, backed by jack pressure; the rapid device includes a load cell, and bi-directional cell pressure is calibrated to load.
key_points: Horizontal jack, rotation-tolerant connection; load cell preferred with pressure backup
sections.applicability: Measuring load in lateral load tests

sections.title: Measurement of Shaft Displacement
sections.body: [pp. 13-70 to 13-72] Top displacement by dial gauges or LVDTs on a reference beam, possibly long-travel (Figure 13-63) or wire-type linear potentiometers extending several feet; horizontal accelerometers in rapid tests. Displacement along the shaft is important and inexpensive: a grooved inclinometer casing in the cage, with a pre-test baseline profile, gives displacement relative to the bottom (Figure 13-64a); for short shafts the base may move, so adjust to a known point above grade; align one groove pair with loading and place the casing at the neutral axis. Inclinometer profiling needs the load held 20 to 30 minutes; shape accelerometer arrays (MEMS, Rollins et al. 2009; Figure 13-64b) monitor the displaced shape continuously; down-hole accelerometers in the casing measure motion in rapid tests (Figure 13-65).
key_points: Long-travel LVDTs or wire potentiometers at the top
Inclinometer casing in the cage: baseline, groove aligned with load, at neutral axis; hold load 20 to 30 min
Shape accelerometer arrays give continuous profiles; down-hole accelerometers for rapid tests
figures: Figure 13-63: Long Travel Displacement Transducer and Inclinometer Casing
Figure 13-64: Measurements of Lateral Displacement in a Lateral Test Shaft below Grade (a) Inclinometer Profiling (b) Shape Accelerometer Array
Figure 13-65: Down-hole Accelerometer for Displacement Measurement During Rapid Lateral Load Test
sections.applicability: Measuring lateral displacement profiles in load tests

sections.title: Measurement and Interpretation of Strain
sections.body: [pp. 13-72 to 13-73] Sister-bar gauges (the text cites Section 13.2.3.3, as printed) on the near and far sides measure tension and compression to estimate bending moment (Figure 13-66): for an elastic beam M = eps E I / c (Eq. 13-10), c the distance from the neutral axis to the gauge. A reinforced concrete shaft cracks in tension, shifting the neutral axis and changing EI dramatically (Chapters 9 and 12, whose methods are generally conservative on stiffness). Actual EI depends on as-built (in-situ cured, often higher) concrete strength, actual cracking stress, actual modulus, as-built diameter, soil or rock confinement, cage position, actual steel strength (usually above minimum) and any casing left in place. Bending strain-to-moment correlation is therefore unreliable, but strains identify the onset of cracking (tension strains jump) and the location of maximum moment and flexural yielding.
key_points: M = eps E I / c (Eq. 13-10) for an elastic beam only
Cracking shifts the neutral axis; actual EI often above design estimates
Strains reliably show cracking onset and location of maximum moment
equations: Eq. 13-10: M = eps E I / c - bending moment from measured strain for a simple elastic beam; E elastic modulus, I moment of inertia, c distance from neutral axis to the point of strain measurement
figures: Figure 13-66: Strain Gauges to Measure Bending Moments
sections.applicability: Interpreting bending strains in lateral load tests

sections.title: Interpretation of Lateral Test Data
sections.body: [pp. 13-73 to 13-74] Interpretation uses a computational model (Chapter 9) with the known head conditions (typically zero moment and known shear) and best estimates of diameter and nonlinear EI, often somewhat higher than computed by Chapter 9 methods. Compute top load-deflection and deflection and moment versus depth for measured loads, and adjust the p-y soil or rock model until agreement is reasonable; overestimated displacement means a conservative model, and good top agreement with a wrong profile means the resistance distribution is wrong. Underestimating shaft EI overestimates soil strength and stiffness, so model EI appropriately. Then apply the model with production boundary conditions (Chapter 9) and site stratigraphy. Lateral tests should be performed during design; construction-phase programs leave little time to change the design, so the design should then be reasonably conservative in lateral soil properties.
key_points: Back-analyze with the Chapter 9 p-y model, known head conditions and realistic (often higher) EI
Match both top deflection and deflection profile
Underestimated EI inflates soil strength and stiffness
Perform lateral tests during design; otherwise design conservatively
sections.applicability: Calibrating p-y models from lateral load tests

sections.title: Summary
sections.body: [p. 13-74] The chapter gave an overview of load testing techniques, measurements and interpretation strategies for design; with the great recent advances in testing technologies, field load tests offer an opportunity for improved economy and reliability of drilled shaft foundations if used effectively and interpreted appropriately.
key_points: Field load tests improve economy and reliability when used effectively and interpreted appropriately
sections.applicability: Overview of Chapter 13, Field Load Tests.
